sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: The FHWA 4-volume state-of-the-practice report (FHWA-RD-96-016 to -019, 1997) developed a micropile classification on two criteria: philosophy of behavior (design), which dictates the design method, and method of grouting (construction), which defines the grout/ground bond strength (side resistance) that generally controls capacity. The designation is a number for behavior and a letter for grouting.
sections.body: (p. 2-1) In 1997 FHWA published a 4-volume report summarizing the state of the practice for micropiles (FHWA-RD-96-016, -017, -018 and -019; 1997), in which a micropile classification system was developed. It is based on two criteria: (1) philosophy of behavior (design) and (2) method of grouting (construction). The philosophy of behavior dictates the method employed in designing the micropile; the method of grouting defines the grout/ground bond strength (or side resistance), which generally controls micropile capacity. The designation has two parts: a number denoting the micropile behavior (design) and a letter designating the method of grouting (construction).
key_points: Classification developed in the FHWA 4-volume state-of-the-practice report (FHWA-RD-96-016 to -019, 1997)
Two criteria: philosophy of behavior (design) and method of grouting (construction)
Behavior dictates the design method; grouting defines the grout/ground bond strength (side resistance), which generally controls capacity
Two-part designation: a number for behavior (design), a letter for grouting method (construction)
sections.applicability: Origin and basis of the FHWA micropile classification system.

sections.title: Design Application Classification
sections.summary: CASE 1 micropiles are loaded directly, the reinforcement resisting most of the load structurally and the bond zone geotechnically (Figure 2-1); they act individually though installed in groups, and make up at least 90 percent of international applications and virtually all North American projects (Figure 2-3). CASE 2 micropiles are lightly reinforced reticulated networks forming a reinforced soil composite loaded as a whole (Figures 2-2, 2-4); very few have been built in the U.S., and their public-sector use will likely be disallowed until performance data exist.
sections.body: (pp. 2-1 to 2-6) The design of an individual micropile or a group of micropiles differs greatly from that of a network of closely spaced reticulated micropiles. CASE 1 micropile elements are loaded directly, and the micropile reinforcement resists the majority of the applied load (Figure 2-1); CASE 2 elements circumscribe and internally reinforce the soil to theoretically make a reinforced soil composite that resists the applied loads, a reticulated micropile network (Figure 2-2). CASE 1 micropiles can be an alternative to more conventional piles, transferring structural loads to a deeper, more competent or stable stratum; directly loaded piles, for axial (compression or tension) or lateral loading, are CASE 1 elements. The load is resisted structurally by the steel reinforcement and geotechnically by side resistance over the bond zone of the individual micropiles. At least 90 percent of all international applications to date, and virtually all North American projects, have involved CASE 1 micropiles, designed to act individually although they may be installed in groups (typical arrangements, Figure 2-3). The remaining applications are networks of reticulated micropiles forming a reinforced soil mass for stabilization and support, CASE 2 elements: structural loads are applied to the entire reinforced soil mass rather than to individual micropiles, so CASE 2 micropiles are lightly reinforced (conceptual application, Figure 2-4). The design philosophy of an individual CASE 1 micropile is the same as that of a group of CASE 1 micropiles, a closely spaced (typically parallel) arrangement each loaded directly; design of individual and grouped CASE 1 elements is discussed in Chapters 5 and 6. A group of CASE 1 elements should not be confused with a reticulated network (CASE 2), although the geometries may look similar. Very few CASE 2 applications have been constructed in the U.S.; with the trend to high capacity micropiles their future U.S. use appears limited, and for public sector projects they will likely be disallowed until a database of performance data allows a technically sound and safe design procedure.
key_points: CASE 1: loaded directly; reinforcement resists most of the load structurally, side resistance in the bond zone geotechnically (Figure 2-1)
CASE 1 can replace conventional piles, transferring axial (compression or tension) or lateral loads to a deeper, competent stratum
At least 90 percent of international applications and virtually all North American projects are CASE 1
CASE 1 micropiles act individually even when installed in groups (Figure 2-3); individual and group design in Chapters 5 and 6
CASE 2: reticulated network forming a reinforced soil composite, loaded as a whole, lightly reinforced (Figures 2-2, 2-4)
A group of CASE 1 elements is not a reticulated (CASE 2) network, though the geometry may look similar
Very few CASE 2 applications in the U.S.; public-sector use likely disallowed until a performance database exists
figures: Figure 2-1: CASE 1 Micropiles (to sustain axial loads, transferring load through a compressible stratum to a bearing stratum, and lateral loads, moving soil over stable soil; micropiles compared with a drilled shaft) (p. 2-2)

Figure 2-2: CASE 2 Micropiles - Reticulated Micropile Network (composite block of pali radice under a cap beam supporting vertical and lateral loads and lowering the center of gravity of the soil-structure unit) (p. 2-3)

sections.applicability: Deciding whether a micropile scheme is CASE 1 (directly loaded) or CASE 2 (reticulated network) before choosing the design method.

sections.title: Construction Type Classification
sections.summary: Grouting method is typically the most sensitive construction process for grout/ground bond, which varies directly with it. Letters A-D (Figure 2-5): Type A, gravity head only (sand-cement mortar or neat grout); Type B, neat grout under 0.5-1 MPa (72-145 psi) pressure as the temporary casing is withdrawn; Type C, gravity grout then, after 15-25 minutes, one global injection at 1 MPa or more without a packer (France, IGU); Type D, gravity or pressure grout then, after hardening, 2-8 MPa (290-1,160 psi) injections, with packers if needed (IRS). Sub-types 1-3 (Table 2-1) give casing and reinforcement.
sections.body: (pp. 2-6 to 2-8) The method of grouting is typically the most sensitive construction process influencing grout/ground bond capacity, which varies directly with the grouting method. The second part of the classification is a letter (A through D) based primarily on the method of placement and the pressure under which grouting is performed; the use of drill casing and reinforcement defines sub-classifications (Figure 2-5). Type A: grout placed under gravity head only; sand-cement mortars or neat cement grouts can be used; the excavation may be underreamed to increase tensile capacity, though this is not common or used with any other type. Type B: neat cement grout placed into the hole under pressure as the temporary drill casing is withdrawn; injection pressures typically 0.5 to 1 MPa (72 to 145 psi), to avoid hydrofracturing the ground or excessive grout takes and to maintain a seal around the casing during withdrawal where possible. Type C: two steps, (1) neat cement grout placed under gravity head as for Type A, and (2) before the primary grout hardens (after about 15 to 25 minutes) similar grout injected one time via a sleeved grout pipe without a packer (at the bond zone interface) at a pressure of at least 1 MPa (145 psi); this type appears to be used only in France, where it is called IGU (Injection Globale et Unitaire). Type D: two steps similar to Type C, with neat cement grout placed under gravity head (as for Types A and C) and possibly pressurized (as for Type B); after the initially placed grout hardens, additional grout is injected via a sleeved grout pipe at 2 to 8 MPa (290 to 1,160 psi), with a packer inside the sleeved pipe so that specific horizons can be treated several times if required; it is used commonly worldwide and is called IRS (Injection Repetitive et Selective) in France. Table 2-1 adds sub-classifications (e.g., A1, A2, A3) for the drill casing and reinforcement used with each grouting method, also representing the reinforcement required by design (reinforcing bar, casing, none). The combined system is thus based on design application (Case 1 or Case 2), micropile type (A, B, C or D) and grouting method (1, 2 or 3), as printed. Table 2-1 is a classification by type of construction and is not intended for contract specifications.
key_points: Grouting method is typically the most sensitive construction process for grout/ground bond capacity, which varies directly with it
Type A: gravity head only; sand-cement mortar or neat cement grout; underreaming possible but not common
Type B: neat grout under pressure as temporary casing is withdrawn, typically 0.5-1 MPa (72-145 psi), avoiding hydrofracture
Type C: gravity grout, then after about 15-25 minutes one injection via sleeved pipe, no packer, at least 1 MPa (145 psi); France only (IGU)
Type D: gravity (or pressurized) grout, then after hardening injections via sleeved pipe at 2-8 MPa (290-1,160 psi), packer for repeat horizons (IRS); used worldwide
Sub-types 1, 2, 3 (Table 2-1) give drill casing and reinforcement: temporary/unlined, permanent full or partial length, permanent upper shaft only
Table 2-1 classifies construction type; it is not intended for contract specifications
figures: Figure 2-5: Micropile Classification System Based on Type of Grouting (Type A gravity; Type B pressure through casing; Type C single global postgrout; Type D multiple repeatable postgrout with packer) (p. 2-7)
tables: Table 2-1: Details of Micropile Classification Based on Type of Grouting (after Pearlman and Wolosick, 1992): sub-type, drill casing, reinforcement, grout. Type A, gravity grout only (sand/cement mortar or neat cement grout tremied to the base of the hole or casing, no excess pressure): A1 temporary or unlined (open hole or auger) with none, single bar, cage, tube or structural section; A2 permanent full-length casing, the casing itself; A3 permanent casing in the upper shaft only, bar(s) or tube in the lower shaft (may extend full length). Type B, pressure-grouted through the casing or auger during withdrawal (neat cement grout tremied first, then excess pressure, up to 1 MPa (145 psi) typically, on additional grout during withdrawal): B1 temporary or unlined, monobar(s) or tube (cages rare due to lower structural capacity); B2 permanent, partial length, the casing itself; B3 permanent upper shaft only. Type C, primary grout under gravity head then one phase of secondary global pressure grouting (15 to 25 minutes later, similar grout injected through a tube or reinforcing pipe from the head at more than 1 MPa (145 psi)): C1 temporary or unlined, single bars or tube; C2 and C3 not conducted. Type D, primary grout under gravity head (Type A) or pressure (Type B), then one or more phases of secondary global pressure grouting (several hours later, through a sleeved pipe or sleeved reinforcement via packers, as many times as necessary to achieve bond): D1 temporary or unlined, single bars or tube; D2 possible only if a regrout tube is placed full length outside the casing, the casing itself; D3 permanent upper shaft only (p. 2-9)
sections.applicability: Identifying grouting Types A to D and sub-types 1 to 3 when reading bond values or specifications.
